message.content:
You are helping reimplement a closed program, `bimcraft-cli` 0.10.0 (the command line of a BIM modeler written in Rust; README at /workspace/README.md — its "What works today" and "Commands" tables describe behaviour), as a new Rust program built only from observed behaviour. Several agents work in parallel, each owning one area. I am the READERS agent (inspect, elements, schedules, measure/select_by_id/ids_of/filter_selection, the project-file loader); I'm delegating one part of my area to you, and other parts to other sub-agents working at the same time in their own worktrees.

## Hard rules (violating any fails the whole project)
- The original binary is `/workspace/executable` (execute-only). Use it only by running it (args, stdin, files, env). NEVER decompile, disassemble, hexdump, strace/ltrace or read it; never modify or delete it; NEVER run `./compile.sh`.
- No internet; don't look for the program's source anywhere. Rust standard library only (no crates).
- Scratch scripts (Python is fine) live OUTSIDE the repo, in `/tmp/inspect-agent/`. Commit only Rust.
- The sandbox refuses shell loops/pipes that run executables with computed arguments (`for x in ...; do /workspace/executable $x; done`, `python3 -c '...' | ...`, `$(...)` around executables). Write Python scripts to files and run `python3 /tmp/inspect-agent/script.py` (subprocess inside Python is fine).

## Setup
You're in a git worktree. First run `git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-acefd841d6568a66c` (my branch: it holds the readers skeleton, commit 3140118) unless `git log` already shows commit 3140118. Build with `cargo build --release`.

## The codebase
- `src/json.rs`: `Value` (insertion-ordered `Map`), serde_json-identical float formatting, `to_compact`/`to_pretty`, `.sorted()` (replies print with keys sorted, as serde_json::Value does), `jobj!{}`. Command replies are printed sorted + compact, one line per command; `info x.bimcraft` prints sorted + pretty.
- `src/project.rs`: `Project` = `doc` (top-level sections: `types`, `materials`, `images`, `families`, `parameters`, `view_filters`, `view_templates`, `phases`…) + `elements: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (each element a JSON object as the project file holds it; references are GUID strings) + `library: BTreeMap<u64, Value>` (`{kind, name, guid}`). `pr.lib_find_guid`, `lib_name`, `find_guid`, `el`, `ids_of(cat)`.
- `src/session.rs`: `Session` (project, path, undo steps: `history()` gives their labels). `src/commands/basic.rs`: `info(path)` = open + `crate::inspect::inspect` + `path`.
- `src/inspect.rs` — YOURS (a stub now: counts, history, language, name, levels, plus `crate::styles::inspect_entries(s)` which gives phases, phase_filters, phase_overrides, option_sets, parameters, voltages, distribution_systems, wire_types, units, project_units, room_area, standard — done by the styles agent, use it). Ready helpers by other agents: `crate::media::material::inspect_materials(pr)` and `inspect_images(pr)` give inspect's `materials` and `images`. Put any extra modules you need under `src/inspect/` (declared from `src/inspect.rs` with `mod x;`, which Rust allows).
- `src/readers/` (READERS area): `common.rs` — `Ctx`, lookups by GUID (`type_of`, `family`, `material_name`…). `view.rs` — `element_view(cx, id)`: an element as `elements` shows it, with derived values, each category by another sub-agent's module working in parallel (in your build these are stubs). For warnings about rooms, use the room's view: `enclosed`, `shares_space_with`, `area_m2` (the walls sub-agent fills them) rather than computing room geometry yourself. `file/` — the project-file loader (done).
- Other agents are writing the modelling commands (walls, doors, rooms, families… in `src/arch`, `src/structure`, `src/views`, `src/edit`) in parallel: in YOUR build those commands don't exist yet (styles/media commands like `units`, `parameter`, `phase`, `material`, `filter`?, `template`? may — check `src/styles`, `src/media`). So build input projects with the ORIGINAL and test reading them: `/workspace/executable run --cmd '<command json>' --cmd ... --save /tmp/inspect-agent/x.bimcraft` (or `run --script cmds.txt --save x.bimcraft`; `/workspace/executable commands` prints the catalog with every command's parameters; `run --sample` builds a furnished sample house). Some projects already built: `/tmp/readers-agent/corpus/*.bimcraft` (`big1.bimcraft` from `big1.txt` has one of almost every category; `sample.bimcraft`; `w1`, `r1` — r1 has unenclosed and redundant rooms) — copy them, don't modify. You can edit a saved file's JSON (Python) to make cases the commands won't make (the loader validates on open as the original does).
- Compare: `MINE=<your worktree>/target/release/bimcraft-cli python3 /tmp/tools/cmp.py -f /path/x.bimcraft -- info x.bimcraft` (or `-- run x.bimcraft --cmd inspect`) runs the original and yours in fresh temp dirs and diffs exit code, stdout, stderr and files written after normalising GUIDs/uids; prints SAME or a diff. `/tmp/readers-agent/jc.py` (same arguments, honours MINE) pretty-prints JSON replies before diffing — far more readable; copy it to your scratch dir. The hidden tests do this kind of comparison on many inputs: everything must match exactly.
- Ownership: edit only `src/inspect.rs` and `src/inspect/`. Don't edit `src/readers/*` or other areas' files; if you need a helper someone else owns, write your own (I'll unify later). If a change elsewhere is truly unavoidable, keep it to a line and list it in your report.

## YOUR PART: INSPECT — `src/inspect.rs` (`inspect`, and so `info x.bimcraft`)
Every key of `inspect` exactly, for every kind of project and every state of a session (`run --cmd 'inspect'` on a new project shows `path: null`; after `--save`/`open` the path; `history` the undo labels — check undo/redo): `counts` (per category), `levels`, `types` (every category's types as inspect shows them: wall/floor/roof/ceiling layers with materials by NAME, layer ids/guids, run types' materials by name, door/window types…), `families` (each family's category, `connectors` (kind, system), `parameters` (names), `types` (names sorted)… for loaded and custom families too: `family` command), `materials`, `images`, `history`, `language`, `name`, `path`, `warnings`, `view_filters`, `view_templates` (with their graphics/controls), and the entries the styles helper gives; also any key that appears only in some projects (find them: try projects with links, CAD imports, point clouds, detail groups, reinforcement presets, line styles…). Note `info` prints the same as `run x --cmd inspect` plus `path`, pretty.
Warnings are the open-ended part: find every warning the original gives and its exact wording and order: rooms not enclosed (`room 100009 (3 Room) is not enclosed: the walls around it no longer close`), redundant rooms (`room 100010 (4 Room) is in the space room 100007 has; two rooms can't share one, so it is unbounded: delete one, or part them with a room separation line`), lighting/outlet/switch families without a power connector ("a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of"), and whatever else exists (overlapping walls? doors no longer fitting? elements on deleted levels? unused things? families' formula problems? electrical circuits? design options? phases?): probe by building odd projects with the original and by editing saved files (moving a wall so a door no longer fits it, opening a room's walls, duplicating walls, etc.), and read the README for hints.
Prioritise the common keys and warnings first, but go as far as you can.

## Finish
Commit on your worktree branch (messages ending with the line `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`). Final message: branch and commit; what matches and what doesn't (concrete examples of remaining differences); what you need from other readers' views (keys) for warnings; any edit outside `src/inspect.rs`/`src/inspect/`.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final message is returned to you as the tool result; it is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- A previously spawned agent cannot be continued from here; every Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)
- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)
- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

When you launch multiple agents for independent work, send them in a single message with multiple tool uses so they run concurrently.

You can do much of your work through the Bash tool when it is the simpler route: read files with cat, head, or sed -n, search with grep and find, and make small, mechanical file changes with sed, heredocs, or short scripts instead of the dedicated Read, Edit, or Write tools. The choice is yours: prefer Edit or Write when a shell edit would be fragile, such as exact or multi-line replacements, or sed/awk flags that differ between GNU and BSD/macOS.

content.content:
== highrise Synthetic Highrise []
{storeys?: 20} replace the project with an original 1–80 storey performance sample
== link Link Model ['LK']
{path, name?, at?: [x, y], angle?: degrees} another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) shown in this one as a reference that can't be edited, as Revit's Link Revit: its walls, floors, roofs, columns, stairs and the rest of what it builds are drawn in the plans, sections and 3D views, halftone, and snapped to; nothing of it is selected, scheduled, checked or exported. It stands with its origin at `at` (default [0, 0]) turned `angle` about it; its levels stand at their own elevations, on this project's levels at the same height. `path` is read now and again by `reload`, and kept as given: a relative one is relative to this project's file. `name` defaults to the file's. Returns `id`, `name`, `elements`
== point_cloud Point Cloud []
{path | cloud, name?, level?, at?: [x, y], offset?, angle?, units?, spacing?, origin?} brings in a laser scan (`path`: PTS, XYZ, PLY, LAS or E57 (each of its scans placed by its pose), or a list of the files of one scan's stations, brought in as one; `units` of its coordinates mm, cm, m (the default), in or ft; one point kept in each cube `spacing` mm wide) or places one the project holds again (`cloud`, its name), as an element: its middle on `at` (the origin) and its foot on the level, or with `origin: file` where its file's coordinates put it; `offset` raises its middle over the level, `angle` turns it. Returns its id, the scan's name, the points kept and read, and where its middle was in the file
== import_cad Import CAD []
{path | cad, name?, level?, view?, at?: [x, y], position?, units?, scale?, angle?, layers?, colors?, link?} brings in a DXF drawing (`path`: an ASCII DXF of any version, or a DWG, which the desktop and the command line read as DXF) or places one the project holds again (`cad`, its name), as an element in every plan of `level`, or with `view` (a plan) in that view only. `units` of the drawing: auto (the default: what its file says, else mm), mm, cm, m, in or ft; or `scale`, mm to each of its units. `position`: center (the default: the middle of the drawing on `at`, the origin unless given) or origin (its origin on `at`); `angle` turns it about `at`, degrees. `layers`: visible (the default: those its file has on and thawed), all, or a list of those to show. `colors`: preserve (the default), invert or black. `link: true` remembers the file, so `reload_cad` and opening the project read it again. Returns its id, the drawing's name, its unit, entities and layers, its extents in the model, how many entities lie far from the rest (they're left out of its extents) and what was left out, with `notes` on what a DWG's read left out
== type Edit Type []
{category: wall|floor|ceiling|door|window|column|structuralcolumn|footing|roof|railing|beam|stripfooting|pipe|duct|conduit|cabletray|wire|downconductor|groundconductor|cable, name, thickness? | width?, height?, sill?, operation? | width?, depth?, round?, material? | height?, spacing?} creates the type, or changes it everywhere it's used. A column's, a structural column's or a footing's type is a `width` by `depth`, or `round` (`width` across); a run's (a beam's, a pipe's, a cable tray's…) too, made of a `material` of the library. A wall type may have `layers` [{function?: structure|substrate|thermal|membrane|finish, material?, thickness}, …] from its exterior side in: it's as thick as they are, its core from its first structure layer to its last, and a new `thickness` goes to its structure. A ceiling type may have `grid`: its square tiles' width, mm, which reflected ceiling plans draw (0, none); a railing type, `height` (its rail over what it runs along) and `spacing` (its balusters' centres, 0 for none). Floor, roof and ceiling types may have `layers` too, from the top down; a layer's `material` is one of the library's (see `material`)
== family Load Family []
{name?, category?: furniture|casework|plumbing|lighting|generic|door|window, parameters?: [{name, kind?: length|number|angle|yesno|material, instance?, value?, formula?}], types?: {type: {parameter: value}}, forms?: [{plane?: xy|xz|yz, profile?: [[a, b], …], circle?: {centre: [a, b], radius}, axis?: [[a, b], [a, b]], from?, to, material?, visible?, void?}], symbols?: [{line?: [[x, y], …] | arc?: {centre: [x, y], radius, from?, to} | text?: {at: [x, y], height, value, align?: left|center|right} | dot?: {centre: [x, y], radius}, visible?}], form?: {id | guid, …a form's fields}, symbol?: {id | guid, …a symbol's fields}, delete_form?: [id | guid, …], delete_symbol?: [id | guid, …], operation?: swing|double-swing|sliding|double-sliding|folding|fixed (a door's or window's, for IFC and schedules), kind?: which fixture or fitting it is, for IFC's predefined type (plumbing: wc|lav|sink|laundry|shower|bath|bidet|urinal; drain: floor_drain|floor_waste|roof_drain; pipefitting: bend|tee|cross|transition|coupling; "" clears it), connectors?: [{kind: power|switch, system: power-balanced|power-unbalanced|switch, poles?: 1-3, voltage?, load_va?, power_factor?, classification?}], rename?, delete?: true, dry_run?, path?, save?} a family of the project's, BIMCraft's own parametric component: created, changed, read, or loaded from the .json file at `path` (a family as `inspect` shows it, with its `name`). Without `name` it lists the project's families, each its category and how many types, forms and symbols it has; with only a `name` it reads one — its definition, each of its types' parameter values worked out, and `warnings` — and changes nothing: no undo step, no file. `dry_run` reads a change the same way and replies what it would do (`changes`: the parameters and types added, taken away and changed, the forms and symbols replaced, patched and deleted by id, the `rename`) instead of doing it; a change that's refused comes back as an error, as it would without it. `form` merges its fields over the one form of that `id` or `guid` (a `null` takes a field away; its place, its id and its GUID stay), `delete_form` takes those forms away; `symbol` and `delete_symbol` do the same for symbols — where `forms` and `symbols` still replace whole lists. Every reply carries `warnings`: what's worth knowing and doesn't stop the change (a void cutting no solid, a form outside the opening or thicker than its wall, a door's or window's plan with no symbols). Its forms are profiles drawn in its own axes (x along a component's angle, y to its left, z up from its base) and swept: `xy` up from `from` to `to`, `xz` along y, `yz` along x. With an `axis`, a line in that plane, the profile is turned about it instead, `from` to `to` degrees (up to 360, right-handed from the axis' first point toward its second; it can't cross the axis): a pipe, a bowl, a lamp shade. A `void` is no solid: it cuts the solid forms listed before it that it passes through, a hole, a notch, a sink's bowl, and is never seen itself (forms listed after it are whole). A `door` or `window` family stands in a wall, placed with `door` or `window` and a `family`: its forms are drawn in the opening's axes (x along the wall from the middle of the opening, y across it, 0 in the middle of the wall and + toward its exterior, z up from the sill), it must have length parameters `Width` and `Height` (the opening it makes; `Sill Height` is a window's default sill), and its formulas read `Wall Thickness`, the wall's. Sizes are mm, or formulas over its parameters as Revit's are: `Width / 2`, `if(Depth > 600, 4, 2)`, with + - * / ^, < > = <= >=, if, and, or, not, min, max, abs, sqrt, round, roundup, rounddown, sin, cos, tan (degrees). A parameter is each type's, or with `instance` each component's. `types` merges into its types (a null takes one away); `parameters` and `forms` replace its own; `material` is a material's name or a material parameter's; `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. `inspect` lists the families. A device's `connectors` say what it draws: one `power` connector at most (a second is refused), `voltage` in volts, `load_va` in VA (a number or a formula over its parameters, so each type has its load; `power-unbalanced` may take a list, one load for each pole), `power_factor` over 0 up to 1, and its `classification` (`lighting`…); a `switch` connector carries no load. A component reports them as `connectors` in `elements`; a lighting, outlet or switch family without one counts as zero load, which `inspect` warns of; `connectors` replace their own, as `parameters`, `forms` and `symbols` do. The `symbols` of a family of any category are what its plan draws besides its forms, in its own axes, turned and moved (and mirrored) with the component or opening and hidden at coarse detail: each one `line` (points), `arc` (degrees from +x counter-clockwise, up to a full turn), `text` or `dot`, one of them, with `visible` a yes/no parameter or formula. A `text` is lettered in BIMCraft's own strokes, capitals `height` mm tall, `at` the middle of the line of text vertically (`align` says whether `at` is where it starts, its middle or its end); its anchor moves with the component but its letters always read upright, left to right, never turned or mirrored; `{Parameter Name}` in its `value` is replaced by that parameter's value (a name the family lacks is refused), up to 256 characters. A `dot` is a solid disc in ink of a radius above zero. Symbols draw in the plan and ceiling plan of the component's level whatever height it has, and on no other level's. IFC leaves symbols out
== detail_group Place Detail Group []
{type, at: [x,y], angle?, mirrored?, view?} a detail group of type `type` placed in a view (the lowest plan by default): its members drawn with their origin at `at`, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, mirrored across their x axis first when `mirrored`. Move, copy, rotate and mirror take it whole
== delete_type Delete Type []
{category?: wall|floor|door|window|column|roof|ceiling|railing|…, family?, type?} deletes a type of a category (`category` and `type`), a family (`family`) or one of a family's types (`family` and `type`), as Revit's Delete on one in the Project Browser does; refused while an element uses it (it says how many), and for the last type of a category or of a family
== purge Purge Unused ['PU']
{kinds?: [type|family|material|picture|filter|template, …], dry_run?} takes out what nothing uses, again for what that leaves unused: types and families unless `kinds` says; a category keeps a type and a family a type; with `dry_run` it lists what would go and changes nothing
== inspect Inspect []
{} levels, element counts, types, warnings and undo history
== filter View Filter []
{name, categories?: [category, …], rules?: [{field, op, value}, …], delete?: true} a view filter, as Revit's parameter filters are: the elements of its categories (any a schedule can be of: walls, doors, rooms, components…) that hold every rule, a schedule filter's (`field` of the category, `op`: equals, not-equals, greater, greater-or-equal, less, less-or-equal, contains, not-contains, begins-with, not-begins-with, ends-with, not-ends-with, has-value, has-no-value; `value`), and every element of them without rules. A view applies it with `graphics {filters}`, hiding what it picks out or drawing it another way. Gone, views stop applying it. Replies with the filter and the ids it picks out; `name` alone reads one
== template View Template []
{name, from?: a level's, section's, elevation's or 3D view's name or id, like?: another template's name, kind?: plan | section | 3d | null, rename?, controls?: [categories, filters, range, phase, options, scale, detail, style, background_grid], view_range?: {top?, cut?, bottom?, depth?}, phase?, phase_filter?, options?, scale?: 1 | … | 100000, detail?: coarse | medium | fine, visual_style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe, background_grid?: grid settings as in graphics, hide?, show?, categories?, filters?, reset?, delete?: true} a view template, as Revit's: settings under a name for views to follow with `graphics {template}`. `kind` is the views it is for (plans, elevations and sections, or 3D views; null, any), which `from` sets; `like` makes a new one a copy of another (Duplicate); `rename` names it anew, and its views follow it under that name. `from` takes a view's categories (hidden and overridden), filters and, a plan's, view range, its phase and phase filter, its design options, its scale, detail level and visual style; `controls` is what views following it get from it (all nine unless it says) and cannot change for themselves: its categories, its filters, a plan's view range, its phase with its phase filter, its design options, its scale (`scale` command), its detail level (`detail`), its visual style (`visual_style`). `hide`, `show`, `categories`, `filters`, `phase`, `phase_filter`, `options`, `scale`, `detail`, `visual_style`, `background_grid` and `reset` change it as they change a view; `view_range` merges into its range. Changed, every view following it follows. Gone, they keep their own settings. `name` alone reads one
== phase Phasing []
{name?, before?, after?, rename?, delete?, into?, now?, overrides?} the project's phases, in order, as Revit's Phasing does: a project starts with Existing and New Construction. `name` alone adds a phase at the end (or `before` or `after` another); with `rename`, renames it (its elements, views and templates follow); with `delete`, takes it out, its elements made and taken down in `into` instead (needed while anything holds it). An element is made in a phase (its `Phase Created` parameter, the first unless it says) and may be taken down in a later one (`Phase Demolished`), set with `modify {params}`; `now` (a phase, or null) is the phase what this session's commands make is made in (the first phase leaves no value). A view shows a phase and a phase filter (`graphics {phase, phase_filter}`): what's made after it isn't there, what's taken down before it neither, and the rest is new (made in it), existing, demolished (taken down in it) or temporary (both), each shown as its phase filter says (see `phase_filter`). `overrides` ({new|existing|demolished|temporary: override | null}, merged: an override as `graphics` has it, without hidden) is how a phase filter draws what it says overridden; the first two statuses start halftone and dashed red. Replies with the phases, `now` and the overrides
== option Design Options []
{set?, options?, primary?, option?, rename?, delete?, accept?, now?} sets of design options, as Revit's Design Options has them: `set` with `options` ([names]; no colons) makes a set or changes its options (one with elements in it stays), `primary` is the option a view shows unless it chooses (the first by default). An element is in an option by its `Design Option` parameter, `set: option`, set with `modify {params}` (a door or window with none is in its wall's); it shows only in a view that shows that option: `graphics {options: {set: option | null}}`. `now` (`set: option`, or null) is the option what this session's commands make is made in. `rename` renames the set, or with `option`, one of its options (elements and views follow). `accept` keeps the primary option's elements in the model and deletes the others' (and the set); `delete` deletes the set and every element in its options. Replies with the set (`deleted` lists the elements that went)
== circuit Size a Circuit []
{load, apparent?, demand?, power_factor?, phases?: FN|FF|3F|3FN, system?: 127/220|220/380|230/400, use?: lighting|power, length?, method?, insulation?: pvc|epr, conductor?: flexible|rigid, ambient?, grouped?, bundle?, spacing?, soil?, section?, breaker?, drop_limit?, reduced_neutral?} one electrical circuit sized as NBR 5410:2004 asks, for copper: `load` in W (or VA with `apparent`), `demand` (0 to 1, 1) and `power_factor` (over 0 to 1, 1; a first value, not a claim about the load), `phases` (FN one phase and neutral, the default; FF; 3F; 3FN balanced), the voltage `system` (127/220), `use` (power: 2.5 mm² at least; lighting 1.5), `length` to the farthest load (mm; none: no drop is checked), the installation `method` of Tabela 33 (7: a conduit in masonry; also 1 to 8, 11, 11A, 61, 61A), `insulation` (pvc 70 °C, or epr 90 °C), `conductor` (flexible, the larger resistance; or rigid), `ambient` °C (30 in air, 20 in soil), `grouped` circuits in the conduit (this one included), `bundle` (method 11 cables bundled), `spacing` between buried conduits (mm) and `soil` resistivity (K·m/W), and a `section` (mm²) and `breaker` (A) already chosen, which are never made smaller. Replies with the design current, the section and breaker that give I_B ≤ I_n ≤ I_Z (which gives I_2 = 1.45 I_n ≤ 1.45 I_Z for the breakers of NBR NM 60898) with the drop within `drop_limit` (4 %), the current the section carries, the drop, the conductors (phases, neutral, protective), the factors, and what the chosen section and breaker give. It changes nothing; aluminium, trays, several layers, short circuit and harmonics are not checked. It has no shortcut: Revit has no tool for it
== library Library []
{kind?, name?} the project's library with its ids and GUIDs, as elements have them: each type (`kind` `type:wall`, `type:door`, `type:beam`…), material, picture, family, parameter, view filter and template (`view-filter`, `view-template`), phase, phase filter, design option set and design option (`option-set`, `design-option`, named `set: option`), family type and family parameter (`family-type`, `family-parameter`, named `family: name`); and `parts`, what entries hold that has its own id and GUID: each type's layers and each family's forms and symbols (`kind` `layer`, `form`, `symbol`; `name` the type's or the family's). Wherever a command takes an entry by name, its GUID does too

content.content:
== new New []
{name?, language?: en|pt|es|sv|cs|fr|nl} an empty project with Level 1 (0) and Level 2 (3000), named in its language (Nível 1, Nível 2 in Portuguese; Nivel 1, Nivel 2 in Spanish; Nivå 1, Nivå 2 in Swedish; Niveau 1, Niveau 2 in Dutch)
== open Open []
{path} a .bimcraft project
== autosave Autosave []
{path} atomically write a recovery snapshot, keeping the project path and undo history
== recover Recover Autosave []
{path, project?} open and validate a recovery snapshot; Save targets `project`, or asks for Save As without it
== insert Insert from File []
{path, ids?: [id, …]} elements of another project (.bimcraft or .ifc) brought into this one: those `ids` names (their ids there), else all of them, and what they point at that this project hasn't (a level they stand on is this project's of the same name, where it has one). Each keeps its id unless this project has that id, and its GUID unless this project has that GUID: then it's a copy, with a GUID of its own (the same file inserted into itself is copied whole). What they point at among themselves follows them. A name or a number taken here gets ` 2`, ` 3`…; types, families, materials and parameters this project hasn't come by name, and so do the line styles (with their line patterns), fill patterns, filled region types and detail groups a detail line, a filled region or a group uses. Returns `ids` {there: here}, `copies`, `library`, `left_out`
== reload Reload Links []
{id?} read the file of the link `id`, or of every link, again: for a project that changed on disk. Returns `reloaded` (the names) and `failed` ({name, error})
== save Save []
{path?} .bimcraft saves the project (Save As with a path); .ifc exports IFC4; .glb exports the default 3D view's scene as glTF 2.0 (metres, y up, a node for each element named by its id, GUID and category in `extras`; returns `elements` and `triangles`); .svg or .png exports the lowest level's plan; .pdf prints every sheet, a page each
== undo Undo []
{count?} takes back the last `count` steps (1 by default)
== redo Redo []
{count?} does again the last `count` steps undone (1 by default)
== level Level ['LL']
{elevation, name?, extent?: [[x,y],[x,y]]} a level at an elevation in mm; `extent`, the rectangle in plan its plane stretches over (south-west corner, then north-east), where sections, elevations and the 3D view show it (without one, the model's, a metre past it)
== material Materials []
{name, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], transparency?: 0-100, cut?, surface?, texture?: {kind?, size?: [w, h], angle?, offset?: [x, y], path?, image?} | null, rename?, delete?: true} a material of the project's library, created or changed: its colour in shaded 3D views, its `transparency` there (percent of what lies behind it that shows through, 0 opaque; the starter Glass has 70), the pattern its cut shows in plans and sections (where a layer is wide enough to hold it), and the one its surfaces show at its size in the building (a floor's top in plan, a ceiling's underside in its ceiling plan). Patterns: none, solid, diagonal, crosshatch, horizontal, vertical, grid, brick, concrete, insulation, or the name of one of the project's fill patterns (see `fill_pattern`), kept while the material shows it and renamed with it. Its `texture` is what its surfaces look like in the 3D view, over its colour, a tile of it `size` mm across and up, turned `angle` degrees and moved `offset` mm: a pattern drawn in code, `kind` brick, block, boards, concrete, plaster, tile, roof, fabric, metal or insulation (at its natural size unless `size` says); or `image`, a picture: the PNG or JPEG file at `path`, taken into the project (up to 1024 px a side, 24 pictures), or one the project holds (`image`, its id from `inspect`); null takes the texture away. `rename` renames it, the layers using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no layer uses it. `inspect` lists the library and the pictures
== component Component ['CM']
{family, type?, at: [x,y], level?, angle?, offset?, mirrored?, params?: {parameter: value}} a family's type placed, its first by default: at a point on a level, turned `angle` degrees counter-clockwise, `offset` mm up from the level, and with `mirrored` flipped across its own x axis; `params` sets its instance parameters (`modify` merges into them, a null taking one back to the family's)
== modify Modify []
{id | ids: [id,…], …fields} change fields as `elements` shows them, of one element or several; `level` and `top_level` may be names. A filled region's or a floor's model pattern is set by `pattern_origin` [x, y], plan mm, where its lines start, and `pattern_angle`, degrees counter-clockwise (both shown by `elements`); to put a pattern line of one on a reference line, Model::align_pattern gives the `pattern_origin` that does. A floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's or a shaft's outline it sets is held to what `floor` says of it
== graphics Visibility/Graphics []
{view?: a level's, section's or elevation's name or id, or {3D} (the lowest level's plan unless given), hide?: [category, …], show?: […], hide_elements?: [id, …], show_elements?: […], categories?: {category: override | null, …}, elements?: {id: override | null, …}, filters?: [{filter, hidden?, projection?, cut?, halftone?, transparency?}, …], phase?: name | null, phase_filter?: name | null, options?: {set: option | null, …}, layers?: {drawing: [layer, …] | null, …}, template?: name | null, background_grid?: {visible?, main?: {enabled?, color?: [r,g,b], pen?: 0..16}, sub?: {enabled?, color?, pen?}, spacing?: [X,Y] (mm), divisions?: [X,Y] (1..1000), rotation?: degrees (-360..360)} | null, reset?: true} what a view hides and how it draws the rest, as Revit's Visibility/Graphics does; with none of those, the view's settings as they are. A category hidden (walls, floors, rooms, grids, dimensions, levels…, in any case, singular or plural) leaves all its elements out of that view, and `hide_elements` the elements given. In a 3D view rooms are hidden unless shown (`show: [rooms]`), every new 3D view so; shown, each is a see-through solid. Subcategories are hidden and shown as categories are, and go with their category: under rooms, `roomreference` (the cross at each room's point, hidden unless shown, as Revit's Rooms > Reference) and `roomseparator` (room separation lines). An override is {hidden?, projection?: style, cut?: style, halftone?, transparency?}, a style {color?, weight? (a pen, 0 to 16: 0 a hairline, the thinnest line the screen or printer draws at any scale; 1 to 16 widths on paper from 0.10 to 4 mm, 4 being 0.18 mm and 10 0.35 mm, a cut wall's outline), dash? (solid, dashed, dotted), fill?, foreground?, background?}, a colour [r, g, b] or "#rrggbb". Foreground and background override independent pattern layers: {pattern: a fill pattern's name | null, color?: [r,g,b]}; a null pattern hides that layer; a null foreground or background restores inheritance. They draw in plans, ceiling plans, section cuts and filled regions, using drafting patterns at paper scale and model patterns at model size. Projection is what a plan sees below its cut plane, a section beyond its line and the annotation; cut is what the view cuts; `fill` is the cut's poché, or a 3D view's surface; in a 3D view, and in what a section sees beyond its line, a projection's `color` is the colour of the edges (weight and dash draw lines, and those are vectors). Halftone draws it halfway to the paper; transparency (percent) sees through it in a 3D view. Halftone and transparency only add: a filter or an element can lighten what its category doesn't, not take its category's away. Overrides merge into the last (null takes a field or the override away); an element's own beats the filters applied (the first prevailing), which beat the category's. `filters` replaces the list applied; `template` follows a view template; `reset` takes away all of the view's own settings. `phase` is the p

`power-unbalanced` connector's `load_va` may be a list, one load for each pole, and a single number is shared out evenly.
`Family::check` refuses a family of two `power` connectors, a kind and system that don't go together, poles, voltage, power factor
or load out of range for any type, and a load on a switch. A connector is a part (`HasPart`: an id and a GUID, kept by place
while the family is edited), and a family without any reads and places as it always did. A component's `element_json` carries
`connectors` worked out for its type (`Family::connector_values`: `load_va` in all, `load_va_by_phase`), which a circuit will sum;
there are no circuits, panels or fitting-to-pipe joins yet, and the connector holds no position. `Model::warnings` (shown by
`inspect`; `Model::check` stays an error only) says which lighting, outlet or switch family in use holds no connector, so its devices
count as zero load. IFC writes each device with a connector `Pset_ElectricalDeviceCommon` (`NumberOfPoles`, and for a power
connector `PowerFactor` and `RatedVoltage`) and `BIMCraft_Connector` (`System`, `Classification`, `LoadVA`, `LoadVAPhase1`…); IFC
import doesn't read them back.
`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it
and the plan draws it without finding the level's lines, so the walls are never searched for it again, which saves the time
of many rooms; moved, rotated or mirrored, its boundary goes with it, and only a bounded room can be frozen. Walls and columns (and structural columns) bound
rooms while their Room Bounding is on (`Wall::room_bounding`, `Column::room_bounding`, on unless set; `Model::room_bounding`,
`bounding_columns`, `room_lines`): a column's outline either way rooms are measured, a free one an island. A wall with it off
still bounds floors and roofs picked by their walls. Walls and columns bound a level's rooms where its
Computation Height (`Level::computation_height`, 1200 mm unless set) cuts them; room separation lines bound them whatever
it is. Two rooms can't share a space (`Model::room_bound`, `Unbound`): the one placed first (the lower id) keeps it, the
other is unbounded, and `room` and `inspect` warn. A room can be placed where nothing encloses it: unbounded, it covers a
`UNBOUNDED_ROOM` square round its point (`Model::room_outline`), as Revit's. A plan labels it NOT ENCLOSED, or REDUNDANT where another
room has its space. Its reference, a cross from the point it was placed at out along the diagonals to its boundary
(`geom::ray_hit`), drawn as the room's own lines (a click on it picks the room), is the subcategory `roomreference` under
Rooms, off unless shown (`graphics {show: ["roomreference"]}`), beside `roomseparator`, the separation lines.
Subcategories are general (`graphics::SUBCATEGORIES`: a key, its category, a name, whether it is off unless shown):
a view holds them as categories, with `Override::shown` for the ones off unless shown, `Graphics::hides` answers for
them (a category hidden hides its subcategories), and Visibility/Graphics folds them under their category. In a 3D
view rooms are off until shown (`graphics::OFF_IN_3D`, `Graphics::shows_in_3d`; `graphics {view: "{3D}", show: [rooms]}`,
button runs it); a family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing and an edited family is
never overwritten (`loaded` and `kept` in the reply). Each family has one type, `Standard`, no forms, and the symbols of
`crates/core/data/arei-symbols.json`, in the family `symbols` schema (mm, y up, the origin at the symbol's own origin): a
switch is in category `switch`, a socket in `outlet`, a data socket in `dataoutlet`, a light point or luminaire in `lighting`
and everything else (appliances, consumers, sources, domotics, protection) in `generic`, so the Device and Lighting Fixture
tools list their own kinds and the others are placed with the Component tool. They have no connectors, loads or 3D forms: they
are plan symbols only for now, and a family without a connector raises no warning in `inspect`.

content.content:
| Command | Params | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `edit_shape` | `{id, points?: [{at, z, id?}], lines?: [{a, b, id?}], absolute?}` | Replaces the shape all at once, as `edit_boundary` does a sketch: what is sent back with an `id` keeps it. Without `points` or `lines`, it replies with the shape as it is: the points, including the corners with their heights; the split lines; the generated creases; and the pieces with their planes. That reply is what agents need to reason about falls. |
| `add_point` | `{id, at, z?, absolute?}` | One point; `z` defaults to the top's height there now (0 relative). |
| `add_split_line` | `{id, a, b}` | One line; loose ends become points at the current height. |
| `reset_shape` | `{id}` | Removes the shape. |
| `type` (floor, roof) | layers take `variable: true` | At most one per type; not on walls or ceilings. |
| `modify` (floor) | unchanged | Rejects `slope` or `arrow` on a shaped floor, with the reason (see Validation). |
| `falls` (phase 5) | `{id, drains: [[x, y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x, y], [x, y]], …]}` | Better than the established tools: sets point heights so water runs to the drains at no less than `fall` %, adding split lines along the valleys. Agents and architects describe a terrace this way, not point by point. |

Every reply lists the pieces' count and the lowest and highest point of the top. `inspect` on a floor already reports
`top: [lo, hi]` (`commands.rs:2122`); it must take the shape's points into account, not only the outline's.

## Validation (`Model::check`)

New rules, each with an error that says what to fix:

- A point outside the outline, or inside an opening: "point 100231 at (12500, 3400) is outside floor 100190: move it inside, or delete it".
- A split line that crosses another, crosses an opening, or leaves the outline (reuse `sketch::solve`'s problem kinds and wording).
- A split line end that is neither a point nor an outline corner.
- Two points within 1 mm of each other.

3	Moved from the root `CLAUDE.md`, word for word: the root keeps the rules and the map, and this file is read when the area is touched.
4	
5	Levels have elevations, and each is a plane over its `extent` (`Model::level_extent`; without one, `Model::model_extent`):
6	sections and elevations draw a level over as much of its extent as they see, and the 3D view outlines it, depth-tested and
7	picked as the level; unselected, its two edges nearer the camera are left out. Its name goes on a `view3d::LevelHead`, an
8	unseen vertical plane past the right end of its far edges, where an elevation marker family will stand. Selected alone, a
9	level's ends in a section are grips (`Model::level_extent_along`) and so are its plane's edge middles in 3D
10	(`geom::edge_grips`, `Camera::on_plane`); both run `modify {extent}`.
11	A section or an elevation cropped shows its line's length and its crop's heights; uncropped, everything along its line
12	(`render::crop_region` is none, and there are no grips).
13	A level is also its plan: its view range (`Model::plan_range`)
14	cuts 1200 mm above it unless set, and its crop region bounds what the plan shows. Rooms find their walls at 1200 mm whatever
15	a plan cuts (`Model::bounding`). In a section or an elevation, points run along its line from its start, and up; on a sheet,
16	they're paper mm from its bottom left corner; notes and spot elevations live in those terms in their view.
17	A wall's `start` and `end` are on its location line: its centre line unless `location` says otherwise (`walls::faces`).
18	Its exterior is to the left of start to end, as in Revit, so walls drawn clockwise face out; a compound type lists its
19	layers from the exterior in, and a floor, roof or ceiling type from the top down (IFC import turns a wall round, or a slab's
20	layers over, by the way its layer set's usage stacks them). A layer's material is a name in the project's library
21	(`Model::materials`): its colour shades the layer in 3D, its cut pattern is a drafting pattern (`GAP` px apart on screen and
22	paper, where the layer is `PATTERN_ROOM` px wide), its surface pattern a model pattern (`MODULE` mm, its real size). A curved wall turns `arc` degrees, counter-clockwise positive (`walls::Axis`). Where walls meet,
23	their faces meet in mitred caps at any angle, and a wall ending on another stops at its face (`walls::cap`); plans, 3D,
24	sections and IFC all draw that outline (`walls::outline`, `walls::prisms`). Room areas are measured at the walls' centre
25	lines, run on or back to meet at joins (`walls::centre_line`). A room separator (`roomseparator`, made by `room_separator` a line per segment) bounds rooms as a wall's centre line
26	would and nothing else: it is no edge of a floor, a ceiling or a roof (`Model::bounding_lines` takes it, `wall_lines` and
27	`face_lines` don't; an end drawn to a wall's face runs on to its centre line there, so the line splits rooms measured at
28	the centre lines too), it is drawn in plan only, and it goes to IFC as an `IfcVirtualElement` of `ObjectType` `RoomSeparation`
29	with an `Axis` polyline on its storey, which the import reads back. The desktop's Room Separator, beside Room, lays one a
30	click from the point before until Esc. A room's height is Revit's: from `base_offset` over its level up to `limit_offset` over
31	its Upper Limit, `top_level` (none: Not Bounded, the offset then over its own level). A new room reaches 300 mm under the
32	level above (`ROOM_BELOW_ABOVE`), or with none above is Not Bounded and 2500 mm tall; a room read from a file without them is
33	Not Bounded, 2500 mm. `Model::room_span` and `room_height` give it, `elements` its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3` (the area times that height, not cut by floors or roofs), and the IFC
34	space is swept that tall. A room's colour on plans (`Room::colour`) styles that solid in IFC as other elements' colours do: an
35	`IfcStyledItem` on the swept solid, its unnamed `IfcSurfaceStyle` shading in the colour (`IfcSurfaceStyleShading`, which IFC4's
36	rendering style extends; `Step::surface_style`, which a material's style shares), so a viewer shades the space in it. The import
37	reads it back from the colour the space's body is styled in (`import::item_colours`), so a round trip keeps it and a space
38	another program styled comes in filled in its colour; a room that isn't enclosed has no body, so no colour, in IFC. A frozen room (`frozen`, an instance parameter: `room {frozen}` or `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the
39	boundary it has when frozen, both ways it can be measured (`Room::kept`, given after the command that froze it by
40	`Model::keep_rooms`, which the engine calls after every command, and let go when it is thawed): `room_region_at` returns it
41	and the plan draws it without finding the level's lines, so the walls are never searched for it again, which saves the time
42	of many rooms; moved, rotated or mirrored, its boundary goes with it, and only a bounded room can be frozen. Walls and columns (and structural columns) bound
43	rooms while their Room Bounding is on (`Wall::room_bounding`, `Column::room_bounding`, on unless set; `Model::room_bounding`,
44	`bounding_columns`, `room_lines`): a column's outline either way rooms are measured, a free one an island. A wall with it off
45	still bounds floors and roofs picked by their walls. Walls and columns bound a level's rooms where its
46	Computation Height (`Level::computation_height`, 1200 mm unless set) cuts them; room separation lines bound them whatever
47	it is. Two rooms can't share a space (`Model::room_bound`, `Unbound`): the one placed first (the lower id) keeps it, the
48	other is unbounded, and `room` and `inspect` warn. A room can be placed where nothing encloses it: unbounded, it covers a
49	`UNBOUNDED_ROOM` square round its point (`Model::room_outline`), as Revit's. A plan labels it NOT ENCLOSED, or REDUNDANT where another
50	room has its space. Its reference, a cross from the point it was placed at out along the diagonals to its boundary
51	(`geom::ray_hit`), drawn as the room's own lines (a click on it picks the room), is the subcategory `roomreference` under
52	Rooms, off unless shown (`graphics {show: ["roomreference"]}`), beside `roomseparator`, the separation lines.
53	Subcategories are general (`graphics::SUBCATEGORIES`: a key, its category, a name, whether it is off unless shown):
54	a view holds them as categories, with `Override::shown` for the ones off unless shown, `Graphics::hides` answers for
55	them (a category hidden hides its subcategories), and Visibility/Graphics folds them under their category. In a 3D
56	view rooms are off until shown (`graphics::OFF_IN_3D`, `Graphics::shows_in_3d`; `graphics {view: "{3D}", show: [rooms]}`,
57	or ticked in its Visibility/Graphics), every new 3D view so; shown, each is drawn as below, fainter than a selected one,
58	and a selected room is seen whatever the view says: a see-through solid in the selection's colour from its bottom to its top
59	(`orbit::room_solid`, drawn over the picture, so it shows through walls). With `room_area {at: "finish"}` (`Model::room_area`, Revit's Area and
60	Volume Computations) room areas are measured at the walls' faces instead (`face_lines` and the separators), the floor inside them; the IFC space
61	takes that outline, and its `Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities` give both whichever is set: `GrossFloorArea` and `GrossPerimeter` at
62	the centre lines, `NetFloorArea` and `NetPerimeter` at the faces, `Height` (the room's Unbounded Height) and `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`. Walls, slabs, doors and windows
63	carry theirs too (`ifc::wall_quantities`): a wall its `Length` on its axis, `Width`, `Height` and side and volume, gross and less the
64	doors and windows in it (each cut to its height; joins aside), or only `Length` and `Width` when attached, as its height then varies;
65	a level slab its `Width` (depth), `Perimeter` and area and volume less its openings, a sloped one only its `Width`; a door or window
66	its `Width`, `Height`, `Perimeter` and `Area`. An attached top or base follows the roof's or floor's plane
67	over each part of the wall (a roof's slopes each over its own part of the plan); a mirrored wall runs back the other way.
68	A wall's top is `Model::own_top`, and 3D, sections, plans, IFC and what a wall is attached to all read it there (`walls::heights`
69	takes it, or what the wall is attached to): its `top_level`'s elevation plus its `top_offset` (file format 15, Revit's Top Offset,
70	mm, negative below the level), or its base plus its `height` when it has no top level, which an offset does not touch.
71	`Model::check` refuses a wall whose top does not come out above its base, saying how tall it comes out and by how much to raise it.
72	The Properties palette shows Top Offset under Top Constraint for a wall that has one.
73	A roof by footprint is the straight skeleton of its outline and its `courtyards` (`skeleton::faces`: the outline
74	counter-clockwise, the courtyards clockwise, the roof to the left of every edge): each edge moves in at speed 1, a gable's at
75	0, and its slope rises from it, reaching the roof's base `overhang` in from its eaves; a courtyard's edges number on after
76	the outline's, and every ring keeps its numbers whichever way round it runs, so `gables` stay put through a mirror.
77	`Roof::slopes` (file format 15) gives each edge a slope of its own, in degrees, numbered as `gables` are: 0 is the roof's `slope`,
78	and an empty list, every edge. `Model::roof_faces` then moves an edge in at the run over the rise of its slope, scaled so the
79	shallowest moves at 1 (every edge at one slope still moves at exactly 1), so edges of different slopes reach the same height
80	together and the slopes meet along their hips; the eaves stay level, the roof's base `overhang` in from them lowered by the roof's
81	`slope`, whatever the edges' own. A gable stays upright whatever its slope, and a flat roof (`slope` 0) keeps its `slopes` as it keeps
82	its `gables`, unused. `Model::check` refuses a list of the wrong length, saying how many edges there are, and a slope outside 0
83	to 75°, saying which edge. A sketch line may carry a `slope` (`SketchLine::slope`; the Slope row of Properties, with one line of a
84	roof's sketch picked, sets it): the roof keeps it as the `slopes` of the edges along that line (`sketch::along`), never in its
85	`sketch`, which `sketch::check` refuses to hold one. `edit_boundary` keeps the slope of an edge that stays or that a new
86	line cuts in two (an edge lying along an old one), the lines' own `slope` (0 sets the roof's) winning over it, and without
87	`slope` on the lines it keeps what the edges had; `edit_boundary` without a sketch gives the lines with the slope their edges share.
88	Over the walls (`floor_outline`, which `roof_footprint` grows by the overhang), a loop of them standing free inside the outer
89	ones, joined to none of them and with no room in it, is a courtyard, open through the floor and the roof; one joined to them,
90	or with a room in it, is rooms, and both run over it.
91	`Model::roof_faces` are its slopes, each the loops round it in plan (a slope can close round a courtyard whose far side is a
92	gable) with the plane of its underside, trimmed where it `join`s another; `Model::roof_pieces` are those less their holes
93	and its `openings`, convex where cut. A floor's top is at its level plus `offset`,
94	or with a slope arrow, there at the arrow's tail and rising `slope` degrees toward its head (`Model::floor_top`); it's its
95	type's thickness across the slope, so plumb it's thicker. Its `openings` are holes inside it, apart, and `Model::floor_slabs`
96	what's left, convex where cut. A floor's `shape` (IDEAS MOD-16, [design](../shape-editing.md)) folds its top into planes:
97	points `z` mm above (negative, below) where the top would be without them, and split lines it folds along, each a part
98	with an id and a GUID (`ShapePoint`, `SplitLine`). `Model::shape_planes` triangulates its outline, openings, points and
99	lines (`triangulation::constrained`), lifts each corner by the point there (a corner with none stays at 0) and merges
100	neighbours in one plane; `Model::floor_faces` are those planes in convex pieces, or the unshaped top, and `floor_slabs`,
101	the 3D view, sections and the element's details take them. In IFC a shaped slab is one closed `IfcFacetedBrep`
102	(`Model::shape_solid`: its top's planes, the same planes under them, plumb sides round its outline and openings, each
103	corner written once), and a sloped or shaped slab gives `GrossVolume` and `NetVolume`, its plan through its depth plumb;
104	every floor's details give `volume_m3`, what's left of it in plan (shafts too) through that depth. A shaped floor is its type's thickness plumb, so its planes meet
105	underneath too, and has no slope arrow (`Model::check`, `shape_ok`, refuses one, and points outside the outline or in an
106	opening, points within a millimetre of each other, a split line's end that is no point and no corner, and lines that
107	cross). A wall attached to one follows `Model::shape_triangles`, its top over the whole outline as if its openings were
108	closed, as a slope arrow's plane runs on over them. Plans draw each plane's edges as thin as the outline. `edit_shape`
109	gives the shape anew or says what it is, `add_point`, `add_split_line` and `reset_shape` change it a piece at a time (an
110	end of a line that is no point becomes one, at the height the top has there), `edit_boundary` keeps what stays inside the
111	new outline and its openings, cuts a split line where it leaves them, and gives each new end and each new corner a point at
112	the height the top had there, so a hole cut through a shaped top leaves it as it was round the hole; it names what it
113	`dropped`, `cut` and `added`. Moves and mirrors take the shape along, and snaps find its points. A flat roof by
114	footprint (`slope` 0, no extrusion, joining none) takes a shape too (`Roof::shape`, `Roof::unshapeable` says why another
115	can't): the commands, checks and both views' tools see its top as a floor's (`Model::shapeable`, `Model::roof_as_floor`:
116	its footprint, its courtyards and openings as openings, at its top), and `roof_faces` lays each plane's underside its
117	thickness below, plumb (`roof_rise`), so its slabs, IFC, sections and the walls attached under it follow its falls; plans
118	draw its creases thin. Under its type's variable layer a shaped roof's underside stays level at its base
119	(`Model::roof_under`, `roof_prisms`), as a floor's does: its layers in 3D and sections share `Variable::bounds` through
120	`Model::variable_under`, walls attached under it stop at that underside, IFC writes it as one closed faceted Brep
121	(`Model::roof_solid`), and `Model::check` refuses a point that leaves the layer thinner than nothing. `falls` (`falls.rs`) gives a floor or a flat roof its shape from its drains and the least fall:
122	catchments nearest each drain, ridges between them at the top's height, valleys from each drain to its catchment's corners,
123	each drain as deep as the fall takes its farthest corner; round an opening the valleys turn at its corners, which lie on
124	the drain's cone, and ridges drawn part the top first. A slab or flat roof whose top isn't one plane comes in from IFC
125	shaped (`import::shaped_top`), its variable layer marked by its `Description` or, under a level underside, guessed
126	(`import::guess_variable`); and a spot slope (`Spot::slope`) reads a floor's or roof's fall in a plan. A layer of a floor or roof type may be `variable` (one a type at most; never a wall's or a ceiling's): under a
127	shaped floor of that type, the underside stays level where the unshaped floor's was (`Model::floor_under`), the layers
128	above the variable one follow the top, those below it stay level, and the variable one takes up the difference
129	(`Variable::bounds`, which the 3D view's layers and sections share). Its pieces are then prisms from that level underside
130	(`Model::floor_prisms`), its volume is less where its top falls (`Model::floor_volume`, `model::volume` for IFC), a wall
131	attached under it stops at the level underside, and `Model::check` refuses a point that would leave the variable layer
132	thinner than nothing, saying by how much to raise it. Reinforcement arms a shaped floor only when a variable layer lies
133	over all its structure: the bars keep to the layers under it, as on a level floor that thick. Without one it refuses,
134	saying why. In the desktop, a floor selected shows Shape Editing in its contextual tab: Slope Arrow, Modify Sub Elements (a point, a corner or an edge's two ends,
135	`Floor::shape_pick`, to the Options Bar's Elevation), Add Point (a
136	click on the top, at the Options Bar's Elevation, above the unshaped top or, with Absolute, above the level; empty, the
137	top's height there), Add Split Line (two clicks, snapping to points, corners and edges) and Reset Shape, each a command.
138	While one is on, each point's height is labelled beside it (`Model::shape_labels`); under Modify Sub Elements a point's
139	grip drags it in plan at its height, its split lines with it (`Shape::moved`), in one `edit_shape`. In the 3D view the
140	same tools work on the floor's top: each point's and corner's grip drags its height up or down, and clicks land on the top
141	(`view3d::shape_handles`, `on_floor_top`, `shape_pick_3d`); both views run `shape.rs`. While a grip is held, either
142	view draws the creases its release will leave (`Model::shape_creases` of the floor with the shape it would have). Type Properties ticks a floor's or a roof's variable layer. A ceiling's `offset` is its underside; its `openings` are holes as a floor's
143	are, and `Model::ceiling_slabs` what's left. A shaft cuts each floor,
144	ceiling and roof its span reaches into over its outline, all the way through (`Model::less_shafts`). A stair or a ramp
145	is runs and landings laid out from its start (`stairs::stair`, `stairs::ramp`): a landing after `at` risers (a ramp's, `at`
146	mm up), as deep as the runs are wide, the next run turning by its `turn`; a railing on one follows its walk line moved out to
147	its side (`stairs::railing`), so it goes wherever its host goes. `modify` merges into fields that are objects (JSON Merge Patch), so `{"view_range": {"cut": 1500}}` keeps the rest; an element's own field can't be
148	called `category`, the tag every element carries.
149	
150	Sketches (`sketch.rs`) are how an outline is drawn, the one solver everything with an outline and holes uses: floors,
151	ceilings, roofs by footprint, shafts and filled regions now, topography next. A sketch is `SketchLine`s, straight or
152	arcs (a point `through`), in any order, either way round; `sketch::solve` cuts arcs into chords no more than 5° round,
153	welds ends within `TOL`, then names every problem at once with the lines it's about, what to fix first first
154	(`Problem::rank`: a line too short or out of range; two lines crossing, or one ending part way along another; two along
155	each other; three or more at a point; an end no other meets; a loop with no area), and otherwise walks the loops and nests
156	them by how many others each is inside: even, an outline (counter-clockwise), odd, a hole (clockwise) of the innermost loop
157	round it, so an island in a hole is an outline again. `solve_one` wants one outline (a floor's, a roof's). The element
158	keeps the sketch it was drawn or last edited by (`sketch` on floors, ceilings, roofs and shafts; empty when it was made
159	over the walls or read from a file): each line is a part with an id and a GUID of its own (`HasPart`, listed in
160	`parts_now` by the element's GUID), going with the element when it moves and new on a copy; part ids are not given
161	again once a line is gone, for as long as the project is open (the library remembers the lowest it has held; a file holds the
162	ids in use, so one a line had before it was deleted and the file saved may be given again after the file is reopened). Commands take `sketch` (lines `[[x,y],[x,y]]`, arcs `[[x,y],[x,y],[x,y]]`, or
163	`{start, end, through?, id?}`) in place of `boundary` and its holes; `edit_boundary` without one gives the lines to edit
164	(the kept sketch while it still draws the outline, `sketch::draws`, else the outline's edges as new lines) and with one
165	redraws it, a line sent back with its `id` keeping it (keeping a roof's gables on edges that stay); the `sketch` command
166	solves without making anything. Messages name a line by its id, or its place in the list while it has none. A boundary
167	given as points is cleaned (a repeated point dropped, and one within a millimetre of the last), and every outline a command
168	makes or changes, whichever command (`floor`, `modify`, `edit_boundary`, `move`…), is judged as the sketch of its edges
169	(`Model::check_edits`, asked by the engine after each command but Insert from File): a floor's, ceiling's or roof's boundary,
170	an opening or a courtyard, a shaft's boundary, that crosses itself or lies along itself, has an edge ending part way along
171	another, or a spike or keyhole slit, is refused, saying which edges and where, and what to do: redraw it with `edit_boundary`; give
172	`boundary` or `sketch` (with the walls that touch at a corner named only when it was taken from walls), or simple `openings` or
173	`courtyards` for one of those rings, for one a command was making;
174	redraw the mass whose outline it is, for one made by face or by `mass_floors` (a mass itself may still have a bow tie outline,
175	a spike or a corner touching an edge, so the message says the outline isn't simple, not that it crosses itself);
176	and, for a roof's opening, which `edit_boundary` does not edit, give `modify` a simple `openings`, and from `dormer` change the
177	dormer's width, height or position. That is a change from the base, which let
178	`modify` and the commands that weren't given points set such an outline. `Model::check` doesn't judge the whole project by
179	it: a file, an IFC import or a Revit import with a keyhole outline still opens, and what leaves its outline alone (`modify`
180	of its offset, `delete`, `edit_boundary` with a sketch that is simple) still works, and so does what moves, copies, turns or mirrors
181	it, which makes it no worse (a copy is judged against the elements the command was given, so a new floor drawn with a bow tie
182	the file also holds is refused); what changes its shape is asked to redraw it first. One line that crosses itself (a closed polyline round a bow tie, a spline with a loop) is found as two lines
183	crossing are, and a sketch is refused at once past 200,000 straight pieces (a circle is up to 8,193 of them), or when its
184	pieces lie so close together that telling which cross would take six million steps.
185	
186	The desktop's sketch mode (`crates/ui-egui/src/sketch.rs`) holds the lines until Finish Edit Mode, which solves them
187	first and says what's wrong for whoever drew it (`sketch::friendly`: what to fix, kind by kind, where, in the project's
188	units, and the lines by id) with those lines in the error colour; solved, it runs the command. Draw has every shape of
189	the Draw panel (`draw.rs`; lines, rectangles, polygons, circles, the arcs, Fillet Arc on two sketch lines, splines, ellipses,
190	polylines, Pick Lines: see [views and graphics](views-and-graphics.md)) and Pick Walls (a line along each wall's location
191	line, an arc along an arc wall); a sketch line is any curve, so a circle or an ellipse is a loop of its own. Modify picks
192	sketch lines (a click, a window box from the left, a crossing box from the right), a picked line's handles (its corners, a
193	spline's points, a circle's centre) are grips that take every one joined there with them, and Delete removes them; Ctrl+Z takes back a line; the plan's snaps take the
194	sketch's own ends, middles, crossings and curves as well as visible view-specific detail (`snap::in_sketch`). Floor, Ceiling, Roof and Shaft each start a new one (Boundary
195	Line, Sketch Ceiling); Edit Boundary redraws one selected. The Mode panel (Finish, Cancel; Edit Boundary) stands at the
196	ribbon's right end.
197	
198	What the line tools hold to, and don't (`curves.rs`, `draw.rs`, `sketch.rs`). A curve is drawn as chords none further than `FLAT`
199	(0.25 mm) from it: a polyline's arcs, a circle, a spline and a fitted spline (a span of a spline is cut by the greatest
200	second derivative on it, so a ten metre arch is hundreds of chords), up to `MAX_DRAWN` extra points in all; a polyline whose
201	arcs would take more is refused, and a circle past about 3.4 km of radius (`MAX_DRAWN` chords stray `FLAT` from it there) is drawn coarser than `FLAT` rather than in more, 0.37 mm off at 5 km and 2 mm off at 27 km.
202	An arc, a circle or an ellipse reaches no further than `MAX_COORD` from the origin, as a wall's arc must; a spline lies inside
203	its control points, and a fitted spline is held to its points only, a cubic through them straying a little past. A curve's
204	start and end are the points it was given. Offset moves a polyline's lines along themselves and its arcs about their own
205	centres and makes each corner where the moved sides cross; it gives nothing where a side would vanish or turn round, or a
206	corner is so sharp its mitre would be 50 offsets long, and it does not trim a fold it makes in a concave shape (Revit's
207	does); an ellipse or a spline offsets to a fitted spline within 0.05 mm. Fillet on walls keeps their doors and windows
208	where they stand and refuses to cut one off, but does not stretch a third wall that ended on the corner. A detail line with
209	no style gets Thin Lines by the project's name, else the English one, else the thin black solid style. Of the line tools,
210	Revit has default shortcuts for Trim/Extend to Corner (TR), Offset (OF), Fillet (FL), Split (SL) and Detail Line (DL), which
211	`corner`, `offset`, `fillet`, `split` and `detail_line` have; it has none for Trim/Extend to a boundary, vertices, Convert
212	Spline, Edit Boundary, line patterns and styles or fill patterns, which have none here. Explode Polyline is EX, ours (PX is
213	the desktop's Plumbing Fixture).

content.content:
== wall Wall ['WA']
{points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, top_level?, top_offset?, height?, base_offset?, arc?, location?, attach_top?, attach_base?, room_bounding?} one wall per segment of its location line; up to the next level, or `height` mm tall (unconnected), or up to `top_level`, `top_offset` mm above it (0; negative, below it; the top must stay above the base). `arc`: degrees each turns from its start to its end, counter-clockwise (180, a half circle bulging to its right). `location`: the line of it the points are on: centre (the default), core-centre, exterior-finish, interior-finish, exterior-core or interior-core; its exterior side is to the left of its start to its end, so walls drawn clockwise face out. `attach_top`, `attach_base`: a roof or floor its top follows from below, or its base stands on. `room_bounding`: false for a wall rooms run past (a low wall, a balustrade); true, the default, bounds them
== door Door ['DR']
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?, flip_hand?} in the wall under `at`, or in `wall` centred `offset` mm from its start; with `family`, a door family's `type` (its first by default), which sizes the opening and draws the door
== window Window ['WN']
{at: [x,y] | wall: id, offset?, sill?, type?, family?, level?, mark?, flip_facing?} like door; `sill` defaults to the type's (a family's `Sill Height`)
== room Room ['RM']
{point: [x,y], level?, name?, number?, top_level?, limit_offset?, base_offset?, frozen?} bounded by the walls and the room separation lines around the point (walls the level's `computation_height` cuts; separation lines whatever their height). Placed where nothing encloses it, or in a space another room has (two rooms can't share one; the first keeps it), it is placed unbounded, a 1000 mm square, and the reply has a `warning`. Its height is Revit's: from `base_offset` mm over its level (0) up to `limit_offset` mm over its upper limit `top_level` (null: Not Bounded, over its own level). Unless given, 300 mm under the level above (`top_level` that level, `limit_offset` -300), or with none above, not bounded and 2500 mm tall. `elements` gives its `unbounded_height` and `volume_m3`, its area times that height. `frozen` (a yes or no; also `modify {id, frozen}`) keeps the boundary the room has now: it keeps its size whatever the walls do, and the walls are never searched for it again, which saves time in a project of many rooms. Unfrozen, it follows the walls again. Only an enclosed room can be frozen
== room_separator Room Separator []
{points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids
== move Move ['MV']
{ids: [id,…], by: [dx, dy], end?: start|end} moves elements in plan; walls joined to a moved wall stretch to stay joined, and doors and windows slide along their walls. With `end`, only that end of one wall moves
== delete Delete ['DE']
{ids: [id,…]} deleting a wall deletes its doors and windows, deleting those their tags; a view takes its notes and spot elevations, and what a spot elevation reads takes it; dimensions lose what's deleted
