== mass_floors Mass Floors ['MF']
{mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level
== rebar Rebar []
{points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule
== reinforce Reinforce []
{host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam, a footing or a floor and the ends of a column; else the host's Cobrimento or ConcreteCover parameter), `grade` (CA-50), `grade_stirrup` (the stirrups' and ties'), `clearance` (least mm between bars; their thickness, at least 20, unless told). A spacing is the most between bars: they are spread evenly, so the last is where the first is from the other end. Beam: `bottom` and `top` {count, diameter, hook?} (`hook`, the straight leg in mm turned up from the bottom bars and down from the top ones at both ends, or {start, end}); `bottom.bent` {count, angle?, top?} bends `count` of the inner bottom bars up at each end (layer `bent`): they run `top` mm along the top face from each end (a fifth of the length unless told), slope down `angle` degrees (15 to 75, 45 unless told) and run along the bottom, and have no hook; `stirrup` {diameter, spacing, ends?: {length, spacing}, hook?} (`ends` closer in the first and last `length` mm; `hook` a tail in mm at the ends); `skin` {diameter, spacing} up each side between the rows; `anchor` {start?, end?} mm the bars run past the ends (0 flush, none a cover short). Column: `bars` {diameter, x?, y?, hook?, jog?} (`hook`, a leg turned into the section at the foot and the top, or {below, above}; `jog` {by, from_top, slope?} steps the bars in `by` mm toward the axis, starting `from_top` mm below the top and running `slope` mm up for each mm across (6 unless told), to leave room for the column above; bars along each face across its width and across its depth, corners counted, 2 each; a round column takes `count` instead of x and y, evenly round its circle, with hoops of 24 sides), `stirrup`, `ties` {diameter, hook?} across a rectangular section between bars that are not at a corner (`hook`, a tail in mm at each end), `anchor` {below?, above?}. Footing: `mesh` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (hook turns the ends up; a round footing's bars stop at its circle). Floor: `bottom` and `top` {x?, y?: {diameter, spacing}, hook?} (bars along east and north; `hook`, a leg turned up from a bottom mesh and down from a top one), stopping a cover sh
== detail Detail Level []
{view, detail?: coarse | medium | fine} how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts: coarse, one poché and openings as their gaps; medium, compound layers with the lines between them and an opening's leaf, swing and glass; fine (the default), the layers' patterns and a floor's surface pattern too. Without `detail` it only says what the view has
== favorite Favorites []
{action?: list|save|load|delete, kind?: material|family, name?, as?, replace?, path?} the user's favorites, kept in a file of their own (`path`; by default in their configuration folder) for every project to use: `save` the project's material or family `name` (a material with the picture its texture is made of, a family with the materials it is made of), under another name with `as`; `load` a favorite into the project, under another name with `as`, or over one it has already with `replace`; `delete` one from the favorites; `list` them (the default)
== paint Paint ['PT']
{id | ids, face?, material} paints a face of the elements with a material of the library, as Revit's Paint does: its colour and texture show in the 3D view over what their types are made of. `face`: a wall's `exterior` or `interior`, a floor's, roof's or ceiling's `top` or `bottom`, and `all` for a column, a component, a door, a window, a stair, a ramp or a railing; without it, every face the elements have. `material` null takes the paint off
== symbol_set Load Symbol Set []
{set: arei, names?: en|nl|fr} loads a set of families that are plan symbols and nothing else, each of one type `Standard` with no forms: `arei` is the Belgian AREI/RGIE's graphical symbols (Table 2.23: switches, sockets, light points, appliances, sources, domotics, protection), 76 families, switches in the switch category, sockets in outlet, luminaires in lighting and the rest generic. `names` is the language of their names, English, Dutch or French as the source prints them; as given none, French in a French project and English otherwise. A family the project has by that name stays as it is, so loading twice changes nothing; the reply lists `loaded` and `kept`. Place them as components
== create_group Create Group ['GP']
{ids, name?} a detail group made of detail lines, filled regions and text notes of one view, as Revit's Create Group: they become type `name`'s members (Group 1, 2… unless told), and one group of it takes their place, its origin the middle of them. Place it again with detail_group; ungroup gives its members back. Returns {id, name}
== repeating_detail Repeating Detail []
{type, start: [x,y], end: [x,y], spacing, mirrored?, view?} detail group `type` repeated along the line from `start` to `end`, every `spacing` mm from `start` (at most 2000 of them), each turned along the line, as Revit's Repeating Detail Component: brick coursing, blocking, batt ties. A view draws up to 10000 group members in all (a repeat places each member of the type again), so a type of 100 members repeats up to 100 times. Returns {id, count}
== group_type Detail Groups []
{name?, rename?, delete?: true} a detail group type: `rename` renames it, its groups following; `delete` takes it away while none of it is placed. Without `name`, it lists each with its members and how many are placed
== work_plane Work Plane []
{view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). Any of them may be moved `offset` mm along its normal (up, for a level; 0 unless given), and may lie at any angle, upright too: what a tool may sketch on it is up to the tool (a floor, a ceiling, a roof and a shaft need a level plane, and stand on the highest level at or below it). Given only `offset`, the plane as it is is moved by that instead. Given nothing, it's the lowest level again, as it is until set. A level deleted takes its work plane with it. Says the plane: a point of it (`origin`), its `normal`, its height at the origin where it isn't upright (`z`) and its `slope` in degrees from level

content.content:
== cad_layers CAD Layers []
{id, hide?: [layer, …], show?: [layer, …], view?} a CAD import's layers, each with its colour and linetype and whether it's shown; `hide` and `show` change which it shows in every view, or with `view` in that view only (its Visibility/Graphics, by the drawing's name)
== reload_cad Reload CAD []
{cad} reads a linked CAD drawing's file again, so every import of it shows what the file holds now (opening the project does too). Returns whether it changed
== reinforcement_preset Reinforcement Presets []
{name?, kind?: beam|column|footing|floor, params?, rename?, delete?: true} a named set of the parameters `reinforce` takes for one kind of host (`params`: its `cover`, `grade`, `grade_stirrup`, `clearance` and what its kind takes, and not `host`), kept in the project; `reinforce` with `preset` takes it and lets what is given with it replace its own. Without `name`, lists them. It is not checked against any host until it arms one
== text_type Text Types []
{name?, font?, size?, bold?, italic?, underline?, width_factor?, color?, border?, border_offset?, border_pen?, like?, rename?, delete?: true} a text type of the project's: its `font`, any the system has, or one BIMCraft carries (IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono, BIMCraft Lettering: single-stroke capitals); Arial, the default, letters on any system (where it isn't installed, Liberation Sans, Arimo, Helvetica or the like stands in, else IBM Plex Sans), and a font a file names that this system hasn't is stood in for likewise. Its capitals' height on paper (`size`, mm, 2.5 for a new one), bold, italic and underlined or not (a family's own bold and italic faces where it has them), `width_factor` (1: as the font draws it), its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), and whether a border is drawn round its notes, `border_offset` mm on paper out from their text (where a leader starts too; 1), in pen `border_pen` (0 to 16; 1). A new one starts as `like` says, or as 2.5mm Arial. A project starts with 2.5mm, 3.5mm and 5mm. `rename` renames it, its notes following; `delete` takes it away while no note is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type, the fonts this system has, and the font that letters each type here (`drawn_with`)
== dimension_type Dimension Types []
{name?, like?, rename?, delete?: true, …values} a dimension type of the project's, as Revit's type parameters, lengths mm on paper. Graphics: `string` continuous|baseline|ordinate (Dimension String Type; baseline lines `baseline_spacing` apart, 7), `tick` diagonal|arrow|open_arrow|dot|none, `tick_size` (2), `line_pen` and `tick_pen` (0 to 16; 4 and 7), `color` ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b]), `line_extension` past the outer witness lines (0.8), `witness` gap_to_element|fixed (Witness Line Control), `witness_length` when fixed (5), `witness_gap` off what it measures (0.6), `witness_extension` past the dimension line (0.8), `centre_mark` on radial and diameter ones. Text: `font` (as text types take; Arial), `text_size` (2.5), `bold`, `italic`, `underline`, `width_factor` (1), `text_offset` off the line (1), `background` opaque|transparent, `read` up_then_left|up_then_right (Read Convention), `units` (mm, cm, m, in, ft, ft-in; null for the project's) and `decimals` (0 to 6; null as the units show), `radius_symbol` (R), `diameter_symbol` (Ø), `equality_text` (EQ). A new one starts as `like` says, else as the default. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial` (aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in it) and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial` (radial and diameter ones). `rename` renames it, its dimensions following; `delete` takes it away while no dimension is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type
== line_pattern Line Patterns []
{name?, segments?: [{dash: mm} | {space: mm} | "dot" | {dot_length: mm} | {offset: {length, count, distance}} | {wave: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {zigzag: {length, frequency, amplitude}} | {text: {length, size, text}}, …], rename?, delete?: true} a line pattern of the project's: 1–32 freely ordered graphic segments, each 0.05–100 mm long on paper, so it reads the same at any scale. Offsets have 2–9 lines spaced symmetrically; frequency is cycles per segment, 0.1–100; amplitude and spacing are mm. Text uses bundled IBM Plex Sans, size is maximum capital height (shrinks to fit length), 1–256 single-line characters, following the curve. All graphics preserve the centerline. A project starts with Dash, Long Dash, Dot, Dash Dot, Hidden and Centre; Solid is a line with none. `rename` renames it, the line styles using it following; `delete` takes it away, while no style uses it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern
== line_style Line Styles []
{name?, pen?, color?: "#rrggbb" | [r, g, b], pattern?: name | "Solid", rename?, delete?: true} a line style of the project's, as Revit's: the pen (0, a hairline, to 16) its lines draw in, their colour (black unless told) and their line pattern. A new one needs `pen`; one changed keeps what it isn't given. A project starts with Hairline, Thin Lines, Medium Lines, Wide Lines, Hidden Lines, Centre Lines and Overhead Lines. `rename` renames it, the lines drawn in it following; `delete` takes it away, while no line is drawn in it. Without `name`, it lists every style
== fill_pattern Fill Patterns []
{name?, target?: drafting|model, lines?: [{angle, spacing, origin?: [x, y], shift?, dashes?: [mm, -mm, …]}, …], drawn?: scale | null, rename?, delete?: true} a fill pattern of the project's, as Revit's (and a PAT file's): families of parallel lines, each at `angle` degrees through `origin`, its lines `spacing` apart and each `shift` along from the last, whole or dashed (`dashes`: a dash's length, a space's as a negative one, 0 a dot); no lines, it fills solid. A drafting pattern's lengths are mm on paper, the same at any scale; a model pattern's mm in the building. A project starts with Solid fill, Diagonal Up and Down, Crosshatch, Diagonal Crosshatch, Horizontal, Vertical, Sand, Brick 225 x 75 and Tile 300. `rename` renames it, the region types filling with it following; `delete` takes it away while no type uses it. `drawn` is the scale (1 : n, its n) of the view one made of lines (`make_fill_pattern`) was drawn in: such a one given a new `target` and no `lines` is rescaled, a drafting one being the drawing on paper at that scale; null forgets it. Without `name`, it lists every pattern
== filled_region_type Filled Region Types []
{name?, foreground?: pattern | null, foreground_color?, background?: pattern | null, background_color?, masking?, rename?, delete?: true} a filled region type of the project's: its foreground pattern over its background one, each in its colour ("#rrggbb" or [r, g, b], black unless told), over the paper when `masking` (it hides what's under it). A new one starts with none. A project starts with Solid Black, Diagonal Up, Crosshatch, Sand, Brick and Masking. `rename` renames it, its regions following; `delete` takes it away while no region is of it. Without `name`, it lists every type
== line_weights Line Weights []
{model?: [{scale, widths}, …], annotation?: [16 widths], reset?: true} the project's line weights, as Revit's Manage > Line Weights: what each pen draws on paper, mm. `model` gives, whole, the model's pens 1 to 16 at each of its scales (1 to 32 of them, 1 : `scale`): a view draws its walls, doors, patterns and the rest of the model in the column of the scale nearest its own (by how many times finer or coarser; the finer of two as near). `annotation` gives the 16 pens that dimensions, tags, text, grids, levels and marks draw in, at any scale. Each width is 0.01 to 20 mm; pen 0 is always a hairline. `reset` goes back to what a project in its units starts with (the model's pens wider at finer scales; at 1 : 100, pen 4 is 0.18 mm and pen 10 0.35 mm). Without any, it says what they are, each scale named as the project's units name it, and `own` whether the project has set them
== object_styles Object Styles []
{categories?: {category: {projection?: pen, cut?: pen}, …}, reset?: true} the project's object styles, as Revit's Manage > Object Styles: the pen (0, a hairline, to 16) each model category draws its lines in where it is seen (`projection`) and where a view cuts it (`cut`), in every plan and section; a view's Visibility/Graphics overrides them. A category given keeps the pen it isn't given. The rest of an element's lines keep their own: a compound wall's layers, a door's jambs, a stair's walk line. `reset` goes back to what a project starts with (cut pen 10 and seen pen 4; a door's and a window's cut 6, a railing seen 6, a mass 4 both). Without either, it says each model category's, `own` whether the project has set it apart

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Collect every warning the original's `info` gives over many files; group by shape."""
import sys, os, re, json, subprocess, tempfile, shutil, collections
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
ORIG = '/workspace/executable'
files = [l.strip() for l in open(sys.argv[1]) if l.strip()]
def info(f):
    d = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix='aw')
    try:
        shutil.copy(f, d)
        p = subprocess.run([ORIG, 'info', os.path.basename(f)], cwd=d, capture_output=True, timeout=120)
        if p.returncode != 0: return f, None
        return f, json.loads(p.stdout).get('warnings', [])
    except Exception as e:
        return f, None
    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(d, ignore_errors=True)
shapes = collections.defaultdict(list)
with ThreadPoolExecutor(8) as ex:
    for f, ws in ex.map(info, files):
        if not ws: continue
        for w in ws:
            s = re.sub(r'room \d+ \(.*?\) is', 'room N (..) is', w)
            s = re.sub(r'room \d+ has', 'room N has', s)
            s = re.sub(r'family `.*?`', 'family `F`', s)
            s = re.sub(r'\d+', 'N', s)
            shapes[s].append((f, w))
for s, l in sorted(shapes.items(), key=lambda x: -len(x[1])):
    print(len(l), s)
    for f, w in l[:2]:
        print('     ', f, '|', w[:300])
